Planefag here. There seems to be a misunderstanding of what that link is showing. That is not radar you are looking at. Some background: Most civilian aviation aircraft (with a few exceptions for ultralights, hot air balloons, etc) have ADS-B transponders. These send out a beacon once per second containing the aircraft's tail number, GPS derived position, altitude, heading, and probably some other data I am not familiar with.

These beacons are received on the ground at air traffic centers to augment the actual radar. The map you are seeing is the output of these transponders. They are also received by nearby aircraft for collision avoidance systems.

There are some internet sites that will filter flights and aircraft at the request of the owner, so some of the more "public" plane tracking sites may not show everything. Now to make this more fun, these beacons are receivable by ANYONE within a hundred miles line of sight to the aircraft. There are several hobbyist that use RaspberryPi's to collect this data and send it in to a central server where you can view it. Check out www.adsbexchange.com for more info.

Military aircraft: In combat situations, do you want your enemy to know your location ? Course not. Most will fly with these turned off unless they are operating in US civilian airspace. Even then, it's up to the pilot to turn it on.
